question: Ari has searched their library this turn with [Bog Glider]. During their end step, Nico casts [Mission Briefing]. Can they use it to cast [Archive Trap] from their graveyard for free?
answer:
Yes. Mission Briefing gives Nico permission to cast Archive Trap from the graveyard but does not dictate what it costs, so Nico may apply Archive Trap's own alternative cost and cast it without paying its mana cost, since Ari (an opponent) searched their library this turn.

Why it works:

- Archive Trap reads "If an opponent searched their library this turn, you may cast Archive Trap without paying its mana cost." That's an alternative cost, chosen as part of casting the spell (announcement), and the condition is checked at that moment. The question stipulates Ari searched their library this turn with Bog Glider, so the condition is satisfied for the rest of that turn. Its normal cost is {3}{U}{U}; the alternative cost makes that {0}.
- Mission Briefing ({U}{U}, instant) says to surveil 2, then "you may cast target instant or sorcery card from your graveyard this turn." It grants only permission to cast from the graveyard — it does not grant flashback and does not impose a cost. Because Nico isn't already paying an alternative cost handed out by Mission Briefing, Nico is free to choose Archive Trap's "without paying its mana cost" alternative cost. (This is the well-known difference from Snapcaster Mage: Snapcaster Mage grants flashback, and a flashback cost is itself an alternative cost, so a card cast via Snapcaster Mage must be cast for its flashback cost and can't also use Archive Trap's free cost.)

Practical points for Nico:

- Archive Trap must already be in Nico's graveyard when Mission Briefing is cast, because Mission Briefing's target is chosen during casting, before the surveil 2 happens. A copy of Archive Trap milled by that surveil can't be the target.
- The permission lasts only "this turn," and Archive Trap is an instant (Trap), so Nico needs to cast it before the turn ends — in practice during that same end step, since players don't normally get priority in the cleanup step.
- Timing assumption: I'm reading this as Ari's end step, in the same turn as the search. Either way, all that matters is that the search and the casting of Archive Trap happen in the same turn; if the search had happened on a previous turn, the alternative cost wouldn't be available and Archive Trap would cost {3}{U}{U}.
- Mission Briefing's replacement effect exiles Archive Trap instead of putting it into the graveyard after it resolves (or is countered).

Multiplayer note: with more than two players, any opponent's search satisfies Archive Trap's condition, so Ari's search enables it. Archive Trap targets an opponent to mill thirteen cards, and that target doesn't have to be Ari — Nico may target any opponent. If Ari is somehow Nico's teammate rather than an opponent, the alternative cost is unavailable and Nico would have to pay {3}{U}{U}.

One caveat outside the rules: I'm taking the premise at face value that Bog Glider's ability actually involved Ari searching their library (e.g., a landcycling/tutor effect). If the effect only revealed or moved cards without the word "search," Archive Trap's condition wouldn't be met.

question: In a game of Two-Headed Giant, Antonio activates the last loyalty ability of [Chandra, Hope's Beacon] with X=1. Could they target both Nico and Noah?
answer:
Yes. Chandra, Hope's Beacon's last ability is "−X: Chandra, Hope's Beacon deals X damage to each of up to two targets," and Nico and Noah are two distinct legal targets, so Antonio may choose both. With X=1, Antonio removes 1 loyalty counter from Chandra, Hope's Beacon, and on resolution Chandra, Hope's Beacon deals 1 damage to Nico and 1 damage to Noah.

Why it works:

- "Up to two targets" here is the shorthand for "any target" — each chosen target can independently be a creature, player, planeswalker, or battle. Two different players are perfectly legal choices.
- The only restriction is that the same target can't be chosen twice for a single instance of the word "target." Antonio couldn't pick Nico twice, but Nico and Noah are separate players, so picking both is fine (CR 601.2c).
- X is chosen once, when the ability is activated, and applies to each target separately. X=1 means 1 damage to Nico *and* 1 damage to Noah — it is not 1 damage divided between them.

What this means in Two-Headed Giant specifically: if Nico and Noah are teammates, their team has a single shared life total, and damage dealt to a player causes that player's team to lose that much life. Two separate 1-damage events hit the same shared pool, so their team loses 2 life total. There's no "doubling" or "halving" — each damage event is tracked separately but drains the same life total.

A few notes:

- Targeting is not restricted to opponents. Antonio could legally target their own teammate, or one opponent and one creature/planeswalker/battle, or just a single target (it's "up to two").
- If one of Nico or Noah becomes an illegal target before resolution (hexproof from something like Leyline of Sanctity, for example), the ability still resolves and deals 1 damage to the remaining legal target. If both become illegal, the ability doesn't resolve.
- Damage dealt to a player is never redirected to that player's planeswalkers; that old redirection rule no longer exists.
- The answer is the same whether the game is a standard two-team Two-Headed Giant game or a Two-Headed Giant game with three or more teams — Antonio may freely pick any two different legal targets, even across different teams.

question: Avalyn has no cards in their library and controls a [Keranos, God of Storms]. What happens at the beginning of their draw step?
answer:
At the beginning of the draw step, Keranos, God of Storms does nothing — its triggered ability triggers at the beginning of your upkeep, not your draw step. What happens is just the normal turn-based draw action: the active player attempts to draw from an empty library, fails, and then loses the game the next time state-based actions are checked (which is immediately after the draw, before any player receives priority in the draw step).

Details:

1. Draw step turn-based action (CR 504.1): as the draw step begins, the active player draws a card. This happens automatically, before any player gets priority, and no one can respond to it.

2. Drawing from an empty library (CR 121.3): a player who attempts to draw from a library with no cards in it doesn't lose the game right at that instant. Instead, they lose the next time state-based actions are performed (CR 104.3c, 704.5b). So there's a brief window in which the game state exists with the failed draw recorded, but no player gets priority in between, so nothing can be done about it unless a replacement effect (like Thassa's Oracle-style alternate win conditions or Platinum Angel) or a static effect saying the player can't lose is already in place.

3. About Keranos, God of Storms specifically: its ability reads "At the beginning of your upkeep, reveal the top card of your library. If it's a land card, draw a card. Otherwise, Keranos deals 3 damage to any target." With an empty library, at the upkeep (one step earlier) no card is revealed, so nothing revealed is a land card, and the "otherwise" clause applies — Keranos, God of Storms deals 3 damage to the target chosen when the ability was put on the stack. Note that you must choose that target when the trigger goes on the stack, before you know whether you'll be revealing a land, and if that target is illegal on resolution the whole ability is countered. Importantly, this upkeep trigger doesn't cause a draw with an empty library, so Keranos, God of Storms doesn't kill you during your upkeep; the fatal draw is the ordinary one at the start of the draw step.

4. If you actually meant "what does Keranos, God of Storms do this turn" — the answer is: 3 damage to a target during the upkeep, and then its controller still loses in the draw step from the empty-library draw.

Multiplayer: only the player with the empty library loses; the game continues among the remaining players, and permanents that player controlled leave the game with them. In a two-player game, their opponent simply wins.

One timing caveat: I'm assuming nothing else (an extra draw, a mill, a shuffle-in effect) happens between the upkeep and the draw step. If some effect refills the library before the draw step's turn-based draw, the player draws normally and survives.

question: Abdullah casts [Telemin Performance] targeting Nico. In response, Nico casts [Veil of Summer]. Abdullah responds with their own Veil of Summer. What happens?
answer:
Telemin Performance does nothing — it's removed from the stack on resolution because Nico is no longer a legal target. Abdullah's own Veil of Summer does not save it.

How it plays out, resolving the stack from the top down:

1. **Abdullah's Veil of Summer resolves.** Abdullah draws a card only if an *opponent* of Abdullah cast a blue or black spell this turn. Abdullah's own Telemin Performance (a blue spell) doesn't count, and Nico's Veil of Summer is green, so in a two-player game Abdullah draws nothing. (In a multiplayer game, if some other opponent had cast a blue or black spell earlier this turn, Abdullah would draw.) Abdullah's spells can't be countered this turn, and Abdullah plus Abdullah's permanents gain hexproof from blue and from black.

2. **Nico's Veil of Summer resolves.** Nico draws a card, because an opponent (Abdullah) cast a blue spell — Telemin Performance — this turn. Nico's spells can't be countered, and, critically, Nico and Nico's permanents gain hexproof from blue and from black until end of turn. "Hexproof from blue" means Nico can't be the target of blue spells or of abilities from blue sources that Nico's opponents control.

3. **Telemin Performance tries to resolve.** It's a blue spell controlled by Nico's opponent Abdullah, and its only target is Nico. The target was legal when the spell was cast, but legality is rechecked on resolution. Since every target is now illegal, Telemin Performance doesn't resolve; it's removed from the stack and put into Abdullah's graveyard. Nico reveals nothing, mills nothing, and Abdullah gets no creature.

Why Abdullah's Veil of Summer doesn't help: the "can't be countered" clause only stops a spell or ability that would counter Telemin Performance. A spell failing to resolve because all its targets are illegal is not a countering effect under the current rules — the game rules simply remove it from the stack — so an uncounterable Telemin Performance still fizzles. And Veil of Summer grants hexproof only to its controller and that controller's permanents; it can't strip hexproof from Nico or make Nico a legal target again.

One timing note: this assumes Nico's Veil of Summer actually resolves before Telemin Performance, which is automatic here since it was cast in response. If Nico had instead cast Veil of Summer after Telemin Performance had already resolved, Nico would draw a card off it but the mill-and-steal would have already happened.

question: Athena controls [Teferi, Time Raveler] and Nicholas flashes in [The Wandering Emperor] on Athena's turn. Can Nicholas activate its abilities this turn?
answer:
Yes — Teferi, Time Raveler does not stop Nicholas from activating The Wandering Emperor's loyalty abilities, and The Wandering Emperor's own text lets Nicholas activate them at instant speed during Athena's turn.

First, a flag on the premise: with Athena controlling Teferi, Time Raveler, Nicholas actually *cannot* cast The Wandering Emperor at flash speed. Teferi, Time Raveler's static ability reads "Each opponent can cast spells only any time they could cast a sorcery," which shuts off the flash-like permission The Wandering Emperor grants for *casting* it. So I'll assume one of these is what happened: Teferi, Time Raveler entered the battlefield after The Wandering Emperor was already on the battlefield, Nicholas cast The Wandering Emperor on his own turn at sorcery speed, or some effect put The Wandering Emperor onto the battlefield without casting it. If instead the question is literally "can Nicholas flash it in?" — no, Teferi, Time Raveler prevents that.

Given The Wandering Emperor is on the battlefield under Nicholas's control during Athena's turn:

- Teferi, Time Raveler restricts only the *casting of spells*. It says nothing about activated abilities, so it places no limit on loyalty abilities at all. (Contrast the older Teferi, Mage of Zhalfir / Teferi, Time Raveler confusion — Time Raveler's restriction is spells-only.)
- Normally, a loyalty ability can be activated only during your own main phase when the stack is empty and you have priority, once per turn per permanent. The Wandering Emperor overrides that with its own printed text: "As long as it's not your turn, you may cast The Wandering Emperor and activate its loyalty abilities any time you could cast an instant." A card's own text beats the general timing rule, so Nicholas may activate one loyalty ability during Athena's turn whenever he has priority and could cast an instant.
- Planeswalkers have no "summoning sickness" restriction, so even if The Wandering Emperor just arrived this turn, its loyalty abilities are available.
- Still only one loyalty ability of The Wandering Emperor per turn, and Nicholas must have the loyalty to pay a minus cost.

Multiplayer note: Teferi, Time Raveler's restriction applies to each of Athena's opponents equally, so the answer is the same whether the game has two players or more — any opponent controlling The Wandering Emperor can activate its loyalty abilities at instant speed on someone else's turn, but none of them can cast spells (including The Wandering Emperor) outside their own main phase while Teferi, Time Raveler is on the battlefield.

If one effect reads “You may play an additional land this turn” and another reads “You can’t play lands this turn,” the effect that precludes you from playing lands wins.

question: In a Two-Headed Giant game, how much life does each team begin the game with?
answer:
Each team begins a Two-Headed Giant game with 30 life — not 20 per player and not 40 per team. The team shares that single life total; there are no separate per-player life totals, so any life gain or loss by either teammate adjusts the one shared 30.

Details and related points:

- Two-Headed Giant is a multiplayer variant in which each team of two players shares a turn (both teammates untap, draw, and take actions during the same turn) and shares one life total. A team loses the game when its shared life total is 0 or less.
- This is true no matter how many teams are playing. A three- or four-team Two-Headed Giant game still starts every team at 30; the number of teams doesn't change the starting total.
- Poison is also shared and uses a raised threshold: a team loses when it has 15 or more poison counters, rather than the normal 10.
- Effects that set a player's life total to a specific number, or that refer to "your life total," operate on the team's shared total in this format.
- If you're playing Commander in Two-Headed Giant, the starting life total is likewise 30 per team (not 40 each), and the commander damage threshold remains 21 damage from a single commander, tracked per player who was dealt it.

So at the start of the game, put a single counter/track a single number at 30 for each team.

question: Aldo casts [Lumithread Field] for its morph cost. If Nico wants to counter it with [Spell Burst], what is the mana value of the Lumithread Field on the stack?
answer:
Zero. Lumithread Field cast face down via morph is on the stack as a face-down spell, which has no mana cost, so its mana value is 0. Nico can counter it with Spell Burst by choosing X=0, paying just {U} (plus the optional {3} buyback if desired).

Why: Morph lets you cast a card face down as a 2/2 colorless creature spell with no name, no mana cost, no card types other than creature, no abilities, and no subtypes (CR 707.2), paying {3} regardless of what's printed on the card. That's true even though Lumithread Field is an enchantment when face up — while face down it's a creature spell. An object with no mana cost has a mana value of 0 (CR 202.3b), and the {3} Aldo actually paid, plus Lumithread Field's printed mana cost and its {1}{W} morph cost, are all irrelevant to that calculation.

So Spell Burst with X=0 has a legal target and will counter the face-down Lumithread Field. Note that {X} here is only about matching mana value; casting Spell Burst for X=0 means its total cost is {U} (or {3}{U} if Nico pays buyback to return Spell Burst to hand).

Two related points: if Aldo had instead turned Lumithread Field face up (paying its {1}{W} morph cost), that's a special action that doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to or countered — but turning a permanent face up isn't possible while it's still a spell on the stack. And once Lumithread Field resolves face down, it's a 2/2 colorless creature permanent with mana value 0; if it's later turned face up, it becomes the enchantment with its printed mana cost and corresponding mana value. None of that changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

question: Alexis would like to choose colorless for [Regicide]. Can they?
answer:
No. "Colorless" is not a color, so if Regicide tells a player to choose a color, Alexis must pick one of the five actual colors — white, blue, black, red, or green — and cannot pick colorless.

Why: the Comprehensive Rules define exactly five colors (CR 105.1). Colorless is the absence of color; it is explicitly not a color (CR 105.2a). So any instruction that says only "choose a color" is limited to those five options, and the same goes for related phrasings like "of the chosen color" or "a color of your choice." This is the same reason Alexis couldn't name colorless for effects like Painter's Servant or a protection-granting "choose a color" ability.

The one exception is wording: a card's own text beats the general expectation. Some cards deliberately say "choose a color or colorless" (or "choose a color, then..." with an explicit colorless option). If Regicide's Oracle text actually includes the word "colorless" as an option, then Alexis may choose it — read the card. But absent that explicit permission, colorless is off the table.

I'm assuming here that the choice on Regicide that Alexis is asking about is a "choose a color" instruction. If instead the choice is something else (a card type, a creature type, or targeting a colorless permanent), the analysis changes: for example, nothing stops a spell from targeting or destroying a colorless creature — the restriction is only on naming colorless as if it were a color.

Player count doesn't matter here; the answer is the same in a two-player game and in multiplayer.

question: Alfonso controls [Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass] equipped with [Glaive of the Guildpact] and no Gates. Does it have vigilance and menace?
answer:
No. With zero Gates, Glaive of the Guildpact grants neither vigilance nor menace, so Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass has neither ability (and also gets no stat bonus from the Glaive).

Why: Glaive of the Guildpact's static ability keys off the number of Gates you control. Its power/toughness boost is "+1/+1 for each Gate you control," which with no Gates is +0/+0, and its keyword-granting clause only turns on while you control three or more Gates. That's a continuously-checked static ability, not a one-shot effect \u2014 the game rechecks your Gate count constantly, so the abilities blink on the moment you control the third Gate and blink off again if you drop below three (for example, if a Gate is destroyed mid-combat, Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass loses vigilance and menace immediately, though it stays untapped if it already attacked with vigilance, and blockers already declared stay legal).

Note that one or two Gates isn't enough either \u2014 the threshold is three. "Gate" here means a land with the subtype Gate (Boros Garrison, Gateway Plaza, the RNA/GRN bicycle Gates, etc.), not just any land whose name contains "Gate."

One caveat on the creature itself: I'm relying on Cyclops of One-Eyed Pass having no printed vigilance or menace of its own \u2014 it's a large, cheap red beater whose own text doesn't grant those keywords. If the printed text on your copy does grant a keyword, that printed ability applies regardless of how many Gates you control, since a card's own text works independently of the Equipment's Gate condition.

This answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game \u2014 only Gates *you* control matter, so opponents' Gates never help.

question: Ainsley casts [Tandem Takedown], granting their two [Devoted Hero] +1/+0. Can each Devoted Hero deal damage to a different one of Nolan's creatures?
answer:
No. Tandem Takedown names only one creature you don't control, so both copies of Devoted Hero must deal their damage to that same single creature — you can't split them across two of Nolan's creatures.

Why: Tandem Takedown lets you choose up to two target creatures you control (here, both Devoted Hero) and gives each of them +1/+0, and then those creatures deal damage equal to their power to a single target creature you don't control. The word "target" appears twice for your own creatures' slot but only once for the opposing creature, and all targets are locked in when Tandem Takedown is cast, not on resolution. So Ainsley picks Devoted Hero, Devoted Hero, and exactly one of Nolan's creatures.

Result: each Devoted Hero is 2/2 while Tandem Takedown resolves, and each deals 2 damage to the chosen creature simultaneously — 4 damage total to that one creature. This is noncombat damage dealt by the creatures themselves, so abilities like deathtouch or lifelink on a Devoted Hero would still apply.

A couple of edge cases:
- If Nolan's targeted creature is an illegal target on resolution (it left the battlefield or gained protection/hexproof) but at least one Devoted Hero is still a legal target, Tandem Takedown still resolves: the remaining legal Devoted Hero targets get +1/+0, and no damage is dealt because the damage target is gone.
- If every target is illegal, Tandem Takedown doesn't resolve at all.

Multiplayer makes no difference here: the one damage target just has to be a creature Ainsley doesn't control, and it can belong to any opponent — but it's still only one creature, and both Devoted Hero hit it.

(Assuming the Bloomburrow printing's wording, which has a single "target creature you don't control" for the damage. If a version you're holding reads "each deal damage to target creature an opponent controls" per creature, the same conclusion applies as long as there's only one such target instance printed.)

question: Aaden has 3 [Witch's Familiar] in their graveyard and casts [Izoni, Thousand-Eyed]. After it enters the battlefield but before its trigger resolves, Nyla activates [Sentinel Totem] to exile all cards from Aaden's graveyard. When Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's ability resolves, how many tokens will be created?
answer:
Zero tokens. Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's undergrowth trigger counts creature cards in your graveyard **as the ability resolves**, and by then Sentinel Totem has already emptied Aaden's graveyard, so the ability creates no Insect tokens.

Why:

- Izoni, Thousand-Eyed reads: "Undergrowth — When Izoni, Thousand-Eyed enters the battlefield, create a 1/1 black and green Insect creature token for each creature card in your graveyard." "Undergrowth" is just a keyword flag for abilities that care about the number of creature cards in your graveyard; it doesn't lock in a count early.
- A number like "for each creature card in your graveyard" is determined when the ability resolves, not when it's put on the stack (CR 608.2). Since Nyla activated Sentinel Totem ("{T}, Exile Sentinel Totem: Exile all cards from all graveyards") while the trigger was still on the stack, the three Witch's Familiar cards are in the exile zone — a different zone from the graveyard — when the trigger resolves. Count = 0, so zero tokens.
- The trigger still resolves; it simply does nothing. Izoni, Thousand-Eyed itself is on the battlefield, not in the graveyard, so it never counted itself anyway.

Timing assumption: I'm reading the question as stated — Sentinel Totem's ability was activated and fully resolved after Izoni, Thousand-Eyed entered but before the trigger resolved. If instead Sentinel Totem's ability resolved *after* Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's trigger had already resolved, Aaden would have gotten 3 Insect tokens and they'd stay on the battlefield (exiling graveyards doesn't remove already-created tokens). If Sentinel Totem was activated before Izoni, Thousand-Eyed was even cast, the result is the same as the main answer: 0 tokens.

Multiplayer note: Sentinel Totem exiles all cards from *all* graveyards, including other players', but Izoni, Thousand-Eyed only counts cards in its controller's graveyard, so the answer is 0 whether it's a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Atlas casts [Piracy] and would like to tap all of Nicole's lands but not cast any spells. Can Atlas do this?
answer:
**Yes.** Atlas can tap every one of Nicole's lands for mana and simply let that mana drain away without casting anything. Nothing about Piracy (or the rules generally) forces a player to spend mana they produce.

**Why:**

- Piracy's effect lets Atlas use other players' lands for mana this turn, with the mana restricted to being spent only on casting spells. That restriction limits *what the mana can pay for*, not *whether the ability may be activated*. There is no rule that prevents a player from activating a mana ability whose mana they have no intention of (or ability to) use.
- Tapping a land for mana is a mana ability: it doesn't use the stack and resolves immediately. Atlas may activate mana abilities any time he has priority (CR 605.3a), so once Piracy has resolved he can, holding priority, tap all of Nicole's lands one after another before anyone else can respond — mana abilities can't be responded to.
- The unspent mana just empties from Atlas's mana pool when the current step or phase ends (CR 106.4). There is no mana burn anymore — that rule was removed in 2010 — so Atlas takes no damage and loses no life for wasting it.

**Practical points:**

- The net effect is a one-sided Stone Rain–ish tempo play: Nicole's lands are tapped for the rest of the turn (and can't be tapped again for mana), so she can't use them for instants or flash spells, though they untap normally in her untap step.
- Atlas is the one activating those mana abilities, so any "cost" or side effect of a land's mana ability applies to Atlas — e.g., a City of Brass or Ancient Tomb under Nicole's control would deal its damage to Atlas, and a land that says "add {C}" gives Atlas colorless mana specifically, not generic mana.
- Piracy only grants the use of lands' *mana* abilities. It does not let Atlas activate a nonmana ability of Nicole's lands (a Rishadan Port–style tap ability, for instance).
- **Multiplayer:** Piracy applies to all other players' mana, not just one opponent's, so in a game with more than two players Atlas may tap every opponent's lands, not only Nicole's. In a two-player game the answer is identical, just narrower in scope.

**Timing assumption:** I'm assuming Piracy has already resolved and Atlas is doing this during his own main phase with an empty stack. If instead he tried to tap Nicole's lands while Piracy was still on the stack, he couldn't — the permission doesn't exist until Piracy resolves.

question: Annie controls [Heliod, Sun-Crowned] and casts [Essence Feed]. Can they choose to put Heliod, Sun-Crowned's +1/+1 counter on one of the tokens created by Essence Feed?
answer:
Yes. Annie can put the +1/+1 counter on a Zombie token created by Essence Feed.

Why: Heliod, Sun-Crowned's ability ("Whenever you gain life, put a +1/+1 counter on target creature or enchantment you control") is a triggered ability. It triggers the moment the life gain occurs during Essence Feed's resolution, but a triggered ability isn't actually put onto the stack — and its targets aren't chosen — until the next time a player would receive priority. That doesn't happen until Essence Feed has completely finished resolving, which means both the life gain *and* the token creation have already happened. The Zombie token(s) are on the battlefield and under Annie's control at the moment targets are chosen, so a token is a perfectly legal target for Heliod, Sun-Crowned's trigger, and the target is still legal when the trigger resolves.

This is true regardless of the internal order of Essence Feed's instructions (life gain first, tokens second, or the reverse) — nothing from a spell's resolution goes on the stack mid-resolution, so the tokens always exist before the trigger is put onto the stack.

A few related points:
- Heliod, Sun-Crowned's trigger is not optional and it targets, so if any legal target exists Annie must choose one; a Zombie token is simply one of the options alongside her other creatures and enchantments (including Heliod, Sun-Crowned itself, since it's an enchantment even when it isn't a creature).
- Heliod, Sun-Crowned's trigger works even if Annie's devotion to white is less than five and Heliod, Sun-Crowned therefore isn't a creature — it's still a permanent on the battlefield with that ability. "Devotion to white" counts white mana symbols in the mana costs of permanents she controls.
- Essence Feed's life gain is a single life-gain event, so Heliod, Sun-Crowned triggers once and places one counter, not one per life point.
- Player count doesn't matter here. In a multiplayer game Annie just picks which player Essence Feed's life-loss portion targets; that choice has no bearing on where Heliod, Sun-Crowned's counter can go.

question: Aleah casts [Clash of Titans], can Aleah choose Nixon's [Storm Crow] for both targets?
answer:
**No. Aleah can't choose Nixon's Storm Crow for both targets.** Whichever way a fight-style spell like Clash of Titans is worded, the same creature can't fill both target slots.

Why, in the two ways such a spell is normally templated:

1. **"Two target creatures fight each other."** That's a single instance of the word "target" that requires two targets. Rule 601.2c says the same object can't be chosen more than once for any one instance of the word "target" (the same object may be chosen once for *each separate* instance of the word). So Nixon's Storm Crow can only fill one of those two slots, and Aleah needs a second, different creature on the battlefield or the spell can't be cast at all.

2. **"Target creature you control fights target creature you don't control" (or "...fights *another* target creature").** Here there are two separate instances of "target," but each one has a targeting restriction that Nixon's Storm Crow can't satisfy twice: Aleah doesn't control Nixon's Storm Crow, so it can't be the "creature you control" target, and the word "another" explicitly excludes the creature already chosen.

Either way, Aleah must pick two distinct creatures (and must be able to do so legally, or Clash of Titans can't be cast).

A note on terminology: **fight** means each of the two creatures deals damage equal to its power to the other simultaneously; it isn't combat damage, so Storm Crow's flying is irrelevant — flying only matters for blocking restrictions, not for fights. And a creature can never fight itself; even if some effect somehow pointed a fight at a single creature, no damage would be dealt.

Multiplayer doesn't change this. With more than two players, the only difference is which creatures qualify for a "creature you don't control" slot — any creature controlled by any opponent (Nixon or anyone else) is eligible.

One caveat: I'm not able to recall Clash of Titans's exact printed wording with confidence. If its text explicitly overrides the general targeting rules (for example, by saying something unusual about choosing the same creature twice), the card's own text wins — but no standard fight spell is worded that way, so the answer above holds for every normal templating.

question: Alejandro controls [Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider] and two [Blight Mamba]s. If Alejandro deals combat damage with both Blight Mambas, how many poison counters will Nico get?
answer:
Nico gets 4 poison counters (assuming both Blight Mambas are unblocked and attacking Nico).

Why:

- Blight Mamba is a 1/1 with infect. Infect means damage a creature deals to a player is dealt in the form of poison counters instead of loss of life (CR 702.90b). Each Blight Mamba would normally cause Nico to get 1 poison counter.
- Importantly, damage dealt to a player by a source with infect causes that source's controller to give that player that many poison counters (CR 120.3c). So it's Alejandro who is putting the counters on Nico, not the game or Nico himself.
- Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider says that if you would put one or more counters on a permanent or player, you put twice that many instead. Since Alejandro controls Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider and is the one putting the poison counters, each Blight Mamba's 1 poison counter becomes 2, for a total of 4.

Timing detail: combat damage from both Blight Mambas is dealt simultaneously, so you can treat it either as one event of 2 counters doubled to 4, or as two events of 1 counter each doubled to 2 each. Both readings give the same result: 4 poison counters.

The second half of Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider (opponents put half as many counters, rounded down) is irrelevant here, because Alejandro, not Nico, is the one putting the poison counters on Nico.

Caveats and variations:
- If either Blight Mamba is blocked (and doesn't have trample), that Blight Mamba deals no damage to Nico and contributes 0 poison counters; a single unblocked Blight Mamba would give 2.
- If Alejandro pumps a Blight Mamba (say to 3 power), that Blight Mamba's damage becomes 3 poison counters, doubled to 6.
- In a multiplayer game, each Blight Mamba could be attacking a different player. Only the poison counters caused by damage actually dealt to Nico count toward Nico's total; if only one Blight Mamba is attacking Nico and connects, Nico gets 2.
- A player with ten or more poison counters loses the game as a state-based action, so 4 counters puts Nico nearly halfway there.

question: Andre casts [Abrupt Decay] targeting Nico's 5/5 Horse creature token, then responds by targeting it with [Arcane Denial]. What happens?
answer:
**Abrupt Decay isn't countered — it resolves and destroys the 5/5 Horse token — but Arcane Denial's card-draw effects still happen.**

Step by step:

1. **Abrupt Decay is a legal way to kill the Horse token.** Abrupt Decay reads "This spell can't be countered. Destroy target nonland permanent with mana value 2 or less." A creature token that isn't a copy of another object has no mana cost, and an object with no mana cost has a mana value of 0. The token's 5/5 power and toughness are irrelevant — 0 is 2 or less, so the Horse token is a legal target. (Exception: if the Horse token were created as a *copy* of some other permanent, it would copy that permanent's mana cost and mana value, and could be too expensive to target.)

2. **Arcane Denial can still target Abrupt Decay.** "Can't be countered" does not make Abrupt Decay an illegal target; it only stops the countering itself. So Arcane Denial is not countered on resolution for having an illegal target.

3. **Arcane Denial resolves and does as much as it can.** The "counter target spell" instruction simply fails to do anything to Abrupt Decay. The rest of Arcane Denial still applies: it sets up two delayed triggered abilities that go off at the beginning of the next turn's upkeep — Abrupt Decay's controller (Andre) *may* draw up to two cards, and Arcane Denial's controller draws a card. Those draws happen even though the counter did nothing.

4. **Abrupt Decay then resolves.** The Horse token is destroyed (assuming it isn't indestructible and has no regeneration/replacement shield) and is put into its owner's graveyard. As a state-based action, a token in any zone other than the battlefield ceases to exist.

**On who casts Arcane Denial:** your wording says Andre responds to his own Abrupt Decay. If that's literally the case, Andre is both "its controller" and "you," so at the beginning of the next turn's upkeep Andre may draw up to two cards *and* draws one more (up to three total), and no one else draws. If, as is more likely intended, Nico (or another opponent) cast Arcane Denial, then Andre may draw up to two cards and the Arcane Denial caster draws one. Nothing else about the outcome changes.

**Two-player vs. multiplayer:** no difference here. Abrupt Decay targets a permanent, not a player, and Arcane Denial's draws are tied to specific players (the countered spell's controller and Arcane Denial's controller), so extra opponents don't change anything.

question: Arabella controls [Yixlid Jailer] and casts [Ever After] targeting [Dearly Departed] and [Fugitive Wizard]. Will Fugitive Wizard enter with a +1/+1 counter?
answer:
No. Fugitive Wizard enters the battlefield as a plain 1/1 with no +1/+1 counter.

Why: Yixlid Jailer has the static ability "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." Dearly Departed's relevant ability — "As long as Dearly Departed is in your graveyard, each Human creature you control enters the battlefield with an additional +1/+1 counter on it" — is an ability that functions only while Dearly Departed is a card in a graveyard. Yixlid Jailer strips that ability away (ability-removing effects apply in layer 6), so while Dearly Departed sits in Arabella's graveyard it simply has no abilities at all and generates no replacement effect.

Ever After returns Dearly Departed and Fugitive Wizard to the battlefield simultaneously. Replacement effects that modify how a permanent enters the battlefield have to exist immediately before that entry event, and at that moment Dearly Departed is still a card in the graveyard with its abilities turned off by Yixlid Jailer. Once Dearly Departed is on the battlefield it's no longer affected by Yixlid Jailer, but its counter-granting ability only functions from the graveyard, so it does nothing there either — and in any case that's too late to affect Fugitive Wizard's arrival.

Worth knowing for contrast: without Yixlid Jailer, the answer would be yes. Because the game checks the state just before the simultaneous entry, Dearly Departed would still be in the graveyard at that moment and Fugitive Wizard (a Human) would enter with a +1/+1 counter — and Dearly Departed, itself a Human, would get one too. Yixlid Jailer is the only reason that doesn't happen here.

Timing note: I'm assuming Yixlid Jailer is on the battlefield continuously through Ever After's resolution. If Yixlid Jailer leaves the battlefield (or loses its ability) before Ever After resolves, Dearly Departed's ability comes back on in the graveyard and Fugitive Wizard would enter with the counter. If Yixlid Jailer leaves after Ever After has already resolved, it's too late — Fugitive Wizard is already on the battlefield without a counter.

Player count doesn't matter here: Ever After only reaches Arabella's own graveyard and returns the creatures under her control, so nothing changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

question: Nicholas controls [Solitary Confinement]. Addilyn attacks with [Ranger of Eos] and casts [Skullcrack] targeting themselves. Does Nicholas lose life?
answer:
Yes — assuming Skullcrack resolves before combat damage is dealt, Nicholas takes the combat damage from Ranger of Eos and loses that life (3 life, since Ranger of Eos is a 3/2, if it's unblocked and Nicholas is the player it's attacking).

Why: Solitary Confinement reads in part "Prevent all damage that would be dealt to you." That's a prevention effect — a replacement-style effect that stops damage from being dealt at all. Skullcrack says "Players can't gain life this turn. Damage can't be prevented this turn. Skullcrack deals 3 damage to target player or planeswalker."

The key point is that only the 3 damage is targeted at Addilyn. The first two sentences of Skullcrack are global, untargeted effects that apply to the whole game for the rest of the turn — not just to the player Skullcrack targets. So once Skullcrack resolves, no damage from any source to any player or permanent can be prevented for the rest of the turn, and Solitary Confinement's prevention effect simply does nothing when Ranger of Eos deals combat damage to Nicholas. (Addilyn also takes the 3 damage from Skullcrack themselves, and no player can gain life this turn.)

Solitary Confinement isn't destroyed or turned off in any other way: Nicholas still skips his draw step, and he still has to discard a card at the beginning of his end step or sacrifice it. Only the damage-prevention clause is being ignored.

Timing caveat: I'm assuming Skullcrack was cast and resolved during the declare attackers or declare blockers step, i.e. before the combat damage step. If instead Ranger of Eos's combat damage had already been dealt and prevented by Solitary Confinement, and only then did Addilyn cast Skullcrack, that earlier damage stays prevented — Skullcrack can't retroactively undo it, and Nicholas would lose no life from Ranger of Eos.

Multiplayer note: the answer is the same with more than two players. Skullcrack's "damage can't be prevented this turn" applies to all damage in the game, so it turns off Solitary Confinement's prevention even though Nicholas isn't the target of Skullcrack. It only matters that Nicholas is the player Ranger of Eos is attacking (or the controller of a planeswalker/battle it's attacking, in which case that permanent, not Nicholas, receives the damage) and that Ranger of Eos is unblocked.

question: Armani casts [Hangarback Walker] with X = 3. Can Neriah counter it with [Thoughtbind]?
answer:
No. With X = 3, Hangarback Walker's mana cost {X}{X} is paid as {3}{3}, so while Hangarback Walker is on the stack its mana value (formerly "converted mana cost") is 6 — well above the limit on Thoughtbind, which reads "Counter target spell with mana value 3 or less." Hangarback Walker is therefore not a legal target for Thoughtbind, and Neriah can't even cast Thoughtbind targeting it.

Why the mana value is 6: for a spell on the stack, the value chosen for X is used to determine the spell's mana value (rule 202.3b). Hangarback Walker's cost has the X symbol twice, and the single chosen value of X applies to both symbols, so Armani pays a total of 6 generic mana and the spell's mana value is 3 + 3 = 6. (Everywhere other than the stack — in hand, graveyard, on the battlefield — X is treated as 0, so Hangarback Walker's mana value there is 0, but that's irrelevant to countering it.)

For reference, Thoughtbind is an instant, so Neriah is free to respond to Hangarback Walker; the only obstacle here is the mana value restriction. Neriah could only use Thoughtbind on Hangarback Walker if Armani had chosen X = 0 (mana value 0) or X = 1 (mana value 2); X = 2 already yields mana value 4, which is too much.

This answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game — Thoughtbind's restriction depends only on the targeted spell's mana value, not on player count.

question: Avery casts [Sram's Expertise]. As it resolves, they would like tap the tokens it created to cast [Collective Effort] escalated twice. Can they?
answer:
Yes. Avery can tap two of the three Servo tokens Sram's Expertise just created to pay Collective Effort's escalate cost twice, even though those tokens have summoning sickness.

Why this works:

1. Timing. Sram's Expertise first creates three 1/1 white Servo artifact creature tokens, and then, still during its own resolution, lets Avery cast a spell with mana value 3 or less from hand without paying its mana cost. The Servo tokens are already on the battlefield when Collective Effort is cast, so they're available to be tapped. Collective Effort's mana cost is {1}{W}{W}, mana value 3, so it qualifies.

2. "Without paying its mana cost" only waives the mana cost. Additional costs still have to be paid. Escalate is an additional cost — Collective Effort reads "Escalate—Tap an untapped creature you control" — so Avery pays it once for each mode chosen beyond the first. Choosing three modes means paying escalate twice, which means tapping two different untapped creatures Avery controls (a creature that's already tapped for the first escalate payment can't be tapped again for the second). With three Servo tokens, Avery taps two and has one left untapped.

3. Summoning sickness doesn't matter here. Summoning sickness (not having been under your control continuously since your most recent turn began) only stops a creature from attacking and from activating its own abilities that include the {T} or {Q} symbol in their cost. Escalate's cost is a cost of Collective Effort, not an activated ability of the Servo tokens, so freshly created tokens can be tapped for it — exactly like convoke.

Practical notes: Avery must still choose legal targets for whichever modes need them ("destroy target creature with power 4 or greater" and "destroy target enchantment"); the third mode, putting a +1/+1 counter on each creature Avery controls, needs no target and will still counter up the tapped Servo tokens. If no legal target exists for a targeted mode, that mode can't be chosen. Modes and escalate payments are locked in as Collective Effort is cast, i.e., during Sram's Expertise's resolution; Collective Effort then goes on the stack and resolves after Sram's Expertise finishes.

This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games — the only difference is the pool of legal targets for the destroy modes (any creature or enchantment on the battlefield, regardless of controller, can be targeted).

question: Nikolas controls [Mindcrank]. Ari casts [Vampiric Tutor]. Will the card Ari put on top of their library get milled?
answer:
Yes — the card Ari tutored with Vampiric Tutor will be milled to Ari's graveyard (assuming Ari is an opponent of Nikolas and nothing else intervenes).

Why: Vampiric Tutor resolves in a fixed order — Ari searches their library for a card, shuffles, puts that card on top of the library, and *then* Ari loses 2 life. So by the time the life loss happens, the tutored card is already sitting on top of Ari's library.

Mindcrank reads "Whenever an opponent loses life, that player mills that many cards." That's a triggered ability controlled by Nikolas. It triggers on Ari's 2 life loss, but it doesn't do anything mid-resolution: Vampiric Tutor finishes resolving completely, then the Mindcrank trigger is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority. When the Mindcrank trigger resolves, Ari mills 2 cards — "mill" means putting that many cards from the top of Ari's library into Ari's graveyard. The top card is the tutored card, so it goes to the graveyard along with the next card down.

How Ari can save it: Ari can respond to the Mindcrank trigger while it's on the stack. Anything that draws Ari a card in response (an instant-speed draw, a flash creature with a draw trigger, etc.) will pull the tutored card into hand before the mill happens; Ari would then mill 2 different cards. Note Ari can't respond "between" putting the card on top and losing the life — that all happens during Vampiric Tutor's resolution with no priority in between. Of course, if the tutored card is something Ari wants in the graveyard (a reanimation target, flashback/escape card, Narcomoeba, etc.), Mindcrank is doing Ari a favor.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same. Mindcrank triggers on life loss by any opponent of Nikolas, so as long as Ari is Nikolas's opponent it triggers regardless of the number of players. If there were multiple Mindcranks, or Ari were the controller of Mindcrank rather than Nikolas, that changes things — Mindcrank never triggers on its own controller's life loss.

question: Does Nicole have a chance to cast [Surgical Extraction] after Addison has drawn for turn but before they have a chance to cast a sorcery?
answer:
Yes. Nicole gets a window during Addison's draw step.

How it works: the draw for turn is a turn-based action that happens automatically at the beginning of the draw step, before any player receives priority (CR 504.1). Once the card is drawn, Addison (the active player) receives priority first. Addison can cast instants or activate abilities at that point, but Addison cannot cast a sorcery there — sorceries can only be cast during your own main phase, with an empty stack, while you have priority (CR 307.1). So when Addison passes priority in the draw step, Nicole receives priority and can cast Surgical Extraction, which is an instant.

The draw step can't end until all players pass priority in succession on an empty stack (CR 117.4), so Nicole is guaranteed that opportunity before Addison's precombat main phase begins. Note that once the precombat main phase starts, Addison again receives priority first (CR 117.3a) — so if Nicole waits until then, Addison can cast a sorcery before Nicole ever gets priority in that phase. The draw step is the window Nicole wants.

Practical points:
- Surgical Extraction costs {B/P}, so Nicole can pay 2 life instead of {B} and doesn't need untapped lands.
- Nicole still needs a legal target: a card in a graveyard that isn't a basic land card.
- Nicole also had a window in Addison's upkeep, but that's before the draw, so it can't hit a card Addison just drew (it hits graveyard cards anyway).

Multiplayer difference: in a game with more than two players, priority passes in turn order starting from Addison. Nicole still gets priority during the draw step, just possibly after other nonactive players have had theirs; the answer is unchanged.

Card-specific exceptions worth checking: if Addison controls something like Vedalken Orrery or Leyline of Anticipation ("you may cast sorceries any time you could cast an instant"), that card's text overrides the general sorcery-timing rule, and Addison could cast a sorcery with the priority they hold in the draw step before Nicole ever gets it. Conversely, if Addison controls Teferi, Time Raveler, Nicole could only cast Surgical Extraction at sorcery speed and would have no draw-step window at all.

question: Ashley controls [Frogtosser Banneret]. Will it affect the cost of [Knowledge Exploitation]?
answer:
No. Frogtosser Banneret does not reduce the cost of Knowledge Exploitation, whether Ashley casts Knowledge Exploitation for its normal mana cost or for its prowl cost.

Why: Frogtosser Banneret reads "Goblin spells and Rogue spells you cast cost {1} less to cast." A "Rogue spell" means a spell that has the creature type Rogue. Only creature cards and kindred (formerly tribal) cards can have creature types; instants and sorceries only get spell types such as Arcane, Trap, or Lesson. Knowledge Exploitation is a plain Sorcery with no subtype at all, so it is neither a Goblin spell nor a Rogue spell, even though it is thematically a "Rogue" card and cares about attacking Rogues via prowl.

So the costs stay:
- Normal cost: {3}{U}{U}.
- Prowl cost (available if a Rogue or Faerie — actually, if a creature with one of Knowledge Exploitation's own creature types dealt combat damage to a player this turn; for Knowledge Exploitation the granted prowl cost is {2}{U}): {2}{U}, unreduced.

Note also that even if a reduction did apply, it would only shave generic mana — the {U} symbols could never be reduced away by Frogtosser Banneret.

One related point of confusion: Frogtosser Banneret itself is a Goblin Rogue, so it can help turn prowl on by dealing combat damage to a player, and it will reduce actual Rogue creature spells (and Goblin spells) Ashley casts by {1}. It just has nothing to say about a typeless sorcery like Knowledge Exploitation. This is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Amir casts [Archon of Cruelty], and before it resolves Norah casts [Surge of Salvation]. What happens when the Archon resolves?
answer:
Nothing about Archon of Cruelty's trigger is stopped. Surge of Salvation doesn't interact with Archon of Cruelty at all here.

Why:

1. Order of resolution. Surge of Salvation is cast while Archon of Cruelty is still on the stack, so Surge of Salvation resolves first (last in, first out) and its effects are already active when Archon of Cruelty resolves and enters the battlefield.

2. What Surge of Salvation grants. It gives permanents Norah controls hexproof from multicolored, and creatures Norah controls protection from red and from white, until end of turn. Hexproof from a quality means that object can't be the target of spells or abilities with that quality controlled by opponents. Protection from a quality means the creature can't be Damaged, Enchanted/Equipped, Blocked, or Targeted by things of that quality ("DEBT").

3. Archon of Cruelty is a mono-black creature, so it is neither multicolored, red, nor white — even if its trigger did target one of Norah's permanents, neither grant would apply.

4. More importantly, Archon of Cruelty's triggered ability targets an opponent — a player, not a permanent. Hexproof and protection granted by Surge of Salvation only apply to Norah's permanents/creatures, not to Norah herself, so she can still be chosen as the target.

5. Sacrificing is not prevented by protection or hexproof. A sacrifice doesn't target, doesn't destroy, and doesn't deal damage, so a protected or hexproof creature can still be sacrificed. Norah chooses which creature or planeswalker she sacrifices; if she controls none, that part simply does nothing (the rest still happens).

So when Archon of Cruelty resolves and its enters-the-battlefield trigger resolves with Norah as the target: Norah sacrifices a creature or planeswalker of her choice, discards a card of her choice, and loses 3 life; Amir draws a card and gains 3 life.

Multiplayer note: Archon of Cruelty says "target opponent," so Amir picks one opponent when the trigger goes on the stack. In a two-player game that must be Norah; with more than two players Amir could instead target someone else, and Norah's Surge of Salvation would be equally irrelevant either way. (Amir chooses the target when the ability is put on the stack, i.e., after Archon of Cruelty has already resolved — Surge of Salvation cast earlier can't change that choice.)

One caveat on timing: I'm assuming Surge of Salvation was cast in response to the Archon of Cruelty spell itself and resolved before it. If instead Norah waited and cast Surge of Salvation in response to the enters-the-battlefield trigger, the outcome is identical — the trigger targets a player, and sacrifice ignores protection and hexproof.

question: Adelynn controls [Clockwork Beast] which has one +1/+0 counter on it. They want to activate its ability with X = 8. Can they?
answer:
Yes — Adelynn can announce the ability with X = 8 and pay {8} plus tap Clockwork Beast, but it's a waste: on resolution she'll only be able to put six +1/+0 counters on Clockwork Beast, bringing it to the maximum of seven.

Why:

- Clockwork Beast's ability reads (Oracle) "{X}, {T}: Put up to X +1/+0 counters on Clockwork Beast. This ability can't cause the total number of +1/+0 counters on Clockwork Beast to be greater than seven. Activate only during your turn, before attackers are declared." Nothing in the cost or the ability restricts what value of X may be chosen; X is chosen as part of announcing the activation (step 601.2b, applied to activated abilities via 602.2b), and the only practical limit is Adelynn's ability to actually pay {8}.
- The number of counters actually placed is chosen when the ability resolves, because it says "up to X." With one +1/+0 counter already on Clockwork Beast, the self-limiting clause on the card means she can choose at most six, ending at seven counters (Clockwork Beast becomes 7/4). She could choose fewer, including zero. Any choice above six is simply not a legal choice — the card's own text overrides the generic "do as much as possible" outcome by capping the total.
- So the two mana above what's needed buys nothing. Activating with X = 6 has exactly the same effect for less mana.

Other requirements to actually activate it:

- The cost includes {T}, so Clockwork Beast must be untapped, and Adelynn must have controlled it continuously since her most recent turn began (or it must have haste) — summoning sickness applies to abilities with {T} in the cost.
- The timing restriction limits activation to Adelynn's own turn, at any point before attackers are declared (untap and upkeep are fine, as is the precombat main phase or the beginning of combat step). She can't do it after attackers are declared or on anyone else's turn.

None of this changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer game; the ability only cares about whose turn it is, not about opponents.

question: Naomi has 7 life and controls two [Death's Shadow]s. Angelo uses [Ajani Unyielding] to exile one of the Death's Shadows. What happens next?
answer:
Naomi gains 6 life (going from 7 to 13), and then her other Death's Shadow immediately dies as a state-based action.

Why:

1. Each Death's Shadow is a 13/13 with the static ability "Death's Shadow gets -X/-X, where X is your life total." With Naomi at 7 life, that ability applies in layer 7c and makes each Death's Shadow a 6/6.

2. Ajani Unyielding's -2 ability reads "Exile target creature. Its controller gains life equal to its power." Both parts happen on resolution: the targeted Death's Shadow is exiled first, then the game determines its power. Since that Death's Shadow is no longer on the battlefield, the game uses last known information — its power as it last existed on the battlefield, which was 6 (13 minus Naomi's 7 life). Naomi, as its controller, gains 6 life and goes to 13.

3. Death's Shadow's -X/-X is not locked in; it's recalculated continuously. With Naomi now at 13 life, the remaining Death's Shadow gets -13/-13 and is a 0/0. The next time state-based actions are checked (immediately after Ajani Unyielding's ability finishes resolving, before any player gets priority), a creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner's graveyard. Regeneration and damage-prevention effects don't help, because it isn't dying from damage or destruction.

So Angelo's -2 effectively kills both Death's Shadows: one by exile, one by the life gain. Ajani Unyielding's loyalty also drops by 2 (from 4 to 2 if it had just entered the battlefield); if it were at 1 loyalty he couldn't activate the ability at all, and at exactly 2 it would go to 0 loyalty and be put into the graveyard as a state-based action at the same time the second Death's Shadow dies.

Timing note: Naomi can respond to the ability while it's on the stack (for instance, by sacrificing or bouncing the targeted Death's Shadow, or paying life). If she pays life in response so that she's at a lower total, the exiled Death's Shadow's power will be higher and she'll gain even more life; nothing she does after the ability starts resolving can stop the life gain once it's resolving.

Player count doesn't matter here — Ajani Unyielding's -2 targets a single creature and only that creature's controller gains life, so the result is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

question: Aniyah currently controls Nico's commander. Can Aniyah cast [Fierce Guardianship] for its alternative cost?
answer:
Yes. Aniyah can cast Fierce Guardianship without paying its mana cost, because its condition is simply "If you control a commander" — it doesn't say "your commander."

Why: being a commander is a characteristic of the physical card, assigned by its owner when the game begins, and it travels with that object no matter who controls it. So while Aniyah controls Nico's commander on the battlefield, Aniyah controls a commander, satisfying Fierce Guardianship's alternative-cost condition. The published rulings on this cycle of free spells (Fierce Guardianship, Deflecting Swat, Deadly Rollick, Flawless Maneuver, Obscuring Haze) state explicitly that the commander you control need not be your own.

Details to keep in mind:

- The commander must be a permanent Aniyah actually controls on the battlefield. Nico's commander sitting in the command zone (or in exile, a graveyard, or Nico's hand) does not let Aniyah cast Fierce Guardianship for free, and a token that's merely a copy of a commander isn't a commander.
- The condition is checked as Aniyah begins casting Fierce Guardianship (when alternative costs are applied). If Aniyah loses control of Nico's commander after Fierce Guardianship is already on the stack, Fierce Guardianship still resolves normally — it isn't countered or refunded.
- Fierce Guardianship still needs a legal target: a noncreature spell an opponent controls. In a multiplayer game that can be any opponent's noncreature spell, not just Nico's; with only two players it's simply the other player's spell. Either way, the answer about the alternative cost is unchanged.
- "Without paying its mana cost" means Aniyah pays nothing for the {2}{U} in Fierce Guardianship's mana cost, but any additional costs or cost increases (for example an effect that says spells cost {1} more to cast) must still be paid; such increases can't be dodged by using the alternative cost.
- Aniyah still needs to cast Fierce Guardianship at a legal time — it's an instant, so any time she has priority.

question: Nia controls [Hollowhenge Huntmaster]. Anders casts [Flesh Duplicate]. Can they have it enter the battlefield as a copy of Hollowhenge Huntmaster?
answer:
**Yes.** Flesh Duplicate's copy clause lets it enter as a copy of *any* creature on the battlefield, not just one its controller owns or controls, so Anders may have Flesh Duplicate enter the battlefield as a copy of Nia's Hollowhenge Huntmaster. Anders controls the resulting permanent, even though Nia controls the creature it copied.

How it works:

- The copy choice is made as Flesh Duplicate enters the battlefield (it's a replacement effect applied as part of the resolution of the spell), not as an announced target when the spell is cast. Nobody can respond to the choice, and Nia gets no say in it. Because it isn't targeting, hexproof/shroud on Hollowhenge Huntmaster wouldn't stop it either (protection from blue likewise doesn't stop a copy effect).
- Flesh Duplicate copies the *copiable values* of Hollowhenge Huntmaster — its printed name, mana cost, types, abilities, and power/toughness (plus any other copy effects already applied to it). It does **not** copy counters, Auras/Equipment attached to it, or one-shot effects pumping it, and Flesh Duplicate's own "except" clause still applies on top (the copy is a Horror in addition to its other creature types).
- Because Hollowhenge Huntmaster is a transforming double-faced permanent (a Werewolf-style card with daybound on its front face), Flesh Duplicate copies **only the face that is currently up**. "Transforming double-faced" means one physical card with two faces where the permanent turns over to become the other face; a copy of it is not itself a double-faced card, so it has no other face and **can never transform**. Any later instruction to transform it — including the automatic day/night transform trigger from daybound or nightbound — simply does nothing to Anders's copy.
  - If Hollowhenge Huntmaster is front-face up (day face) when Flesh Duplicate enters, Anders gets a Horror copy of that front face, with daybound, stuck on that face permanently. Note that if it's currently night, the copy is told to transform and can't, so it just stays as the day face.
  - If Hollowhenge Huntmaster has already transformed to its back (night) face, Flesh Duplicate copies that back face instead — including its larger stats and nightbound — and again can't ever turn back.
  - If it's neither day nor night when the copy enters with daybound, it becomes day.
- Timing caveat: if Nia's Hollowhenge Huntmaster leaves the battlefield in response to Flesh Duplicate (in response to the spell, before it resolves), there's nothing to copy and Flesh Duplicate simply enters as its own printed self.

Multiplayer changes nothing here: "any creature on the battlefield" includes creatures controlled by any opponent or teammate, so with three or more players Anders can still pick Nia's Hollowhenge Huntmaster.

One honest caveat: this all hinges on Flesh Duplicate's copy clause reading "any creature on the battlefield." If your printed copy of Flesh Duplicate instead says "a creature **you control**," then the card's own text wins over the general permissiveness of copy effects, and Anders could not copy Nia's Hollowhenge Huntmaster at all. Check the card face before proceeding.

question: Ada casts [Shaman of the Pack]. In response to its trigger, Nickolas kills it with [Foolish Fate]. How much life does Nickolas lose?
answer:
Nickolas loses life equal to the number of Elves Ada controls at the moment the trigger resolves — and Shaman of the Pack itself is no longer among them. So if Shaman of the Pack was Ada's only Elf, Nickolas loses 0 life; if Ada controlled two other Elves, he loses 2.

Why:

- Casting Shaman of the Pack doesn't trigger anything by itself. Its ability is an enters-the-battlefield trigger ("When Shaman of the Pack enters the battlefield, each opponent loses life equal to the number of Elves you control"). So the sequence you describe is: the spell resolved, Shaman of the Pack entered the battlefield, the trigger went on the stack, and Nickolas responded with Foolish Fate.
- Killing Shaman of the Pack does not counter or remove the trigger. A triggered ability on the stack is an independent object; destroying, exiling, or otherwise removing its source has no effect on it. The trigger will still resolve.
- However, "the number of Elves you control" is a value determined as the ability resolves, not when it triggered. Shaman of the Pack is itself an Elf Shaman, so while it was on the battlefield it counted itself. Once it's gone, it isn't counted at resolution, so the life loss is one lower than it would have been.
- Timing note: I'm assuming Foolish Fate finishes killing Shaman of the Pack before the trigger resolves (that's what "in response" means). If instead Nickolas let the trigger resolve first and only then killed Shaman of the Pack, the life loss would include Shaman of the Pack itself.

Multiplayer: the trigger says "each opponent," meaning each of Ada's opponents. Every opponent — Nickolas and anyone else at the table — loses that same amount; it isn't split. Nickolas killing Shaman of the Pack reduces the loss for all of Ada's opponents equally.

One caveat: I can't reliably recall a card named Foolish Fate, so I'm treating it simply as a removal spell that puts Shaman of the Pack into the graveyard (or exile) before the trigger resolves. If Foolish Fate actually does something else relevant — such as bouncing Shaman of the Pack, or having Ada draw or gain something — the Elf count at resolution is still what matters, and the answer above holds for the life-loss question.

question: In a Commander game, how much life does each player begin the game with?
answer:
Each player begins a Commander game with 40 life, instead of the normal 20.

A few related points:

- This applies regardless of the number of players — 40 life each in a two‑player Commander duel and in a typical four‑player free‑for‑all alike.
- The other Commander-specific life rule to remember is commander damage: a player who has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the course of the game loses, even if their life total is still above 0. That total is tracked separately for each commander.
- Two‑Headed Giant Commander is the notable exception to the 40: in that format each *team* has a single shared life total of 30, not 40 per player. Ordinary multiplayer variants (free‑for‑all, Archenemy‑style, etc.) still use 40 per player.
- Brawl, which is a related singleton commander‑style format, is not Commander proper and uses its own starting life total (25 in the standard two‑player version), so don't apply the 40 there.

question: Amina attacks with [Retaliation]. Nico declares no blocks and then casts [Curtain of Light] targeting Retaliation. Does Retaliation trigger?
answer:
**Yes — if Retaliation's ability reads "whenever this creature becomes blocked," it triggers.** Curtain of Light ("Target attacking creature becomes blocked. Draw a card.") changes Retaliation's blocked/unblocked status from unblocked to blocked, and that status change is exactly what a "becomes blocked" ability watches for. The trigger goes on the stack when Curtain of Light finishes resolving and will resolve before the combat damage step.

The one big caveat is the exact wording on Retaliation:

- "Whenever this creature **becomes blocked**" → triggers. No creature has to be blocking it; the status alone is enough.
- "Whenever this creature **becomes blocked by a creature** / **by one or more creatures**" → does **not** trigger. Curtain of Light gives Retaliation zero blocking creatures, so that condition is never met.

Other points that matter here:

1. **Retaliation is now blocked by no creatures.** A blocked creature with no creatures blocking it assigns no combat damage at all — so Retaliation deals no damage to Nico or to anything else, which is the whole point of Curtain of Light. The exception is trample: a creature with trample that's blocked by no creatures assigns all its combat damage to the defending player.
2. **It only happens once.** A creature that is already blocked can't "become blocked" a second time, so if Nico had declared a blocker and then cast Curtain of Light, no new trigger would occur.
3. **Timing assumption.** I'm assuming Curtain of Light is cast in the declare blockers step after "no blocks" was announced, which is the normal play. If it were cast earlier (declare attackers step), Retaliation would still become blocked and still trigger, but Nico could additionally declare real blockers later; if it were cast after combat damage, the trigger would still occur but too late to stop any damage already dealt.
4. **Player count doesn't change this.** Whether it's a two-player game or multiplayer, the ruling is the same — Curtain of Light just needs a legal target among the attacking creatures, and in multiplayer even a player who isn't the defending player can cast it.

One honest note: the card I know named Retaliation is an enchantment, not a creature, so I'm answering on the reading your question implies — Retaliation is the attacking permanent with a "becomes blocked"-style triggered ability. Check its printed text for the "by a creature" clause, since that's the deciding factor, and remember a card's own wording overrides the general expectation.

question: Ariel controls [Rest in Peace] and targets Nataly's [Dauthi Voidwalker] with [Lightning Bolt]. What happens to each card?
answer:
Both cards end up in exile, and Nataly gets no void counter (assuming Ariel makes the choice sensibly).

**Dauthi Voidwalker (the creature):** Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to Dauthi Voidwalker, which is a 2/3. When state-based actions are next checked (after Lightning Bolt finishes resolving), Dauthi Voidwalker has lethal damage marked on it and is destroyed. As it would be put into Nataly's graveyard, Rest in Peace replaces that event and exiles it instead. Dauthi Voidwalker's own replacement ability does *not* apply to itself: it only replaces cards going to an **opponent's** graveyard, and Nataly's graveyard is not an opponent's graveyard from Dauthi Voidwalker's controller's perspective. So Dauthi Voidwalker is exiled with no void counter on it.

**Lightning Bolt (the spell):** As the last step of its resolution, Lightning Bolt is put into its owner's graveyard — Ariel's graveyard. Two replacement effects want to modify that same event:
- Rest in Peace: exile it instead.
- Dauthi Voidwalker: exile it with a void counter instead (Ariel is Nataly's opponent).

This matters because Dauthi Voidwalker is still on the battlefield at that moment — state-based actions aren't checked in the middle of a spell's resolution, so the lethally damaged Dauthi Voidwalker doesn't die until Lightning Bolt has already been put into the graveyard/exile. When multiple replacement effects apply to one event, the affected object's controller chooses which to apply first; Lightning Bolt is on the stack and controlled by Ariel, so **Ariel** chooses. Applying either one changes the destination to exile, after which the other no longer applies (the card is no longer being put into a graveyard). Ariel will choose Rest in Peace, so Lightning Bolt is exiled with **no** void counter, and Nataly can't later sacrifice Dauthi Voidwalker to cast it. (If Ariel perversely chose Dauthi Voidwalker's ability instead, Lightning Bolt would be exiled with a void counter — but that choice is Ariel's, not Nataly's.)

Note also that Rest in Peace's enters-the-battlefield ability already exiled all graveyards when it came down; the part doing the work here is its ongoing static replacement effect, which applies to every player's cards and tokens from every zone.

**Timing caveat:** I've assumed Lightning Bolt is the only thing on the stack and nothing kills Dauthi Voidwalker earlier. If Dauthi Voidwalker had already left the battlefield before Lightning Bolt finished resolving (e.g., Nataly sacrificed it in response), only Rest in Peace would apply to Lightning Bolt, with the same end result: exile, no counter.

**Multiplayer:** The answer is the same with more than two players. Rest in Peace affects everyone's graveyards regardless of who controls it, and Dauthi Voidwalker's ability keys off "an opponent's graveyard," which includes every opponent of Nataly. The only wrinkle would be if the Lightning Bolt's owner were Nataly herself or (in a Two-Headed Giant/teams format) a teammate, in which case Dauthi Voidwalker's ability wouldn't apply at all and Rest in Peace alone would exile it.

question: Ainsley and Noor are starting a two-player game. Ainsley decides to keep their hand of 7 cards. Noor decides to mulligan. Can Ainsley now decide to mulligan?
answer:
No. Once Ainsley has declared that they're keeping their hand, that decision is final — Ainsley cannot change their mind and mulligan just because Noor chose to mulligan.

How the mulligan procedure works (the "London mulligan"): each player draws a hand equal to their starting hand size (normally seven). Then, in turn order beginning with the starting player, each player declares whether they will take a mulligan. After all declarations are made, every player who declared a mulligan does so simultaneously: they shuffle their hand into their library and draw a new hand of seven. This repeats until no player takes a mulligan. A player who has declared "keep" is out of the process and may not take any further mulligans, even though other players are still mulliganing.

So in this game: Ainsley is locked into their seven-card hand. Noor shuffles back and draws a new seven, then decides again whether to keep or mulligan again — Noor may repeat this as many times as they like, and Ainsley simply waits. When Noor finally keeps, Noor puts a number of cards equal to the number of mulligans Noor took on the bottom of their library in any order (one card if Noor mulliganed once). Ainsley took zero mulligans, so Ainsley bottoms no cards and keeps all seven.

One timing note: since declarations are made in turn order starting with the starting player, if Ainsley is the starting player, Ainsley declares first and Noor gets to make their choice knowing Ainsley kept. If Noor is the starting player, Noor declares first — but either way, once Ainsley says "keep," Ainsley is committed. The same rule applies in multiplayer games with more than two players: any number of other players can keep mulliganing, and a player who has already kept never gets another chance to mulligan.

Once each player has made a declaration, all players who decided to take mulligans do so at the same time. To take a mulligan, a player shuffles the cards in their hand back into their library, draws a new hand of cards equal to their starting hand size, then puts a number of those cards equal to the number of times that player has taken a mulligan on the bottom of their library in any order. Once a player chooses not to take a mulligan, the remaining cards become that player’s opening hand, and that player may not take any further mulligans. This process is then repeated until no player takes a mulligan. A player can take mulligans until their opening hand would be zero cards, after which they may not take further mulligans.

question: Anahi casts [Aura Mutation] targeting Nehemiah's [Leyline of the Void]. Will Aura Mutation go to Anahi's graveyard or exile?
answer:
Aura Mutation goes to Anahi's graveyard, not exile (assuming Nehemiah's Leyline of the Void is actually destroyed by it and no other Leyline of the Void or similar replacement effect is on the battlefield).

Why: Leyline of the Void reads "If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead." That's a replacement effect, and it only functions while Leyline of the Void is on the battlefield. A spell is put into its owner's graveyard as the very last step of its own resolution — after all of its instructions have been carried out. So the order is:

1. Aura Mutation resolves and destroys Leyline of the Void. Destruction moves it to Nehemiah's graveyard immediately (its own controller's graveyard, so Leyline of the Void doesn't exile itself — it only replaces cards going to an *opponent's* graveyard).
2. Aura Mutation creates a 1/1 green Saproling token for each point of Leyline of the Void's mana value. Leyline of the Void costs {2}{B}{B}, mana value 4, so Anahi gets four Saprolings (last known information on the battlefield is used).
3. Only then is Aura Mutation itself put into Anahi's graveyard. By that moment Leyline of the Void is no longer on the battlefield, so its replacement effect no longer exists and Aura Mutation is simply put into the graveyard.

Exceptions worth checking: if Leyline of the Void is indestructible, regenerated, or otherwise not destroyed (or if it's already gone when Aura Mutation resolves, making Aura Mutation fizzle for lack of a legal target — a countered-on-resolution spell is put into the graveyard while Leyline of the Void is still out), then Aura Mutation is exiled instead. Likewise if Nehemiah controls a second Leyline of the Void or another effect with the same replacement, Aura Mutation is exiled.

Multiplayer note: in a game with more than two players, if any *other* opponent of Anahi also controls a Leyline of the Void, that one still applies and Aura Mutation is exiled. With exactly two players and only the one Leyline of the Void, Aura Mutation reaches Anahi's graveyard normally.
